ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The MAP study was approved by a Rush University Medical Center Institutional Review Board with the IRB approval number of L86121802.
table.header: DECLARATIONS Ethics approval and consent to participate

table.text: The participants were from the Rush Memory and Aging Project (MAP), an ongoing longitudinal clinical pathologic cohort study recruiting community-dwelling older adults across northeastern Illinois since September 1997.
At annual visits, the participants were asked to walk 8 feet and turn 360 o twice.
Participants were also asked lower back pain and pain in the hip, knee, or feet that had lasted at least one month and had been present in most days.

Participants completed 21 cognitive tests 28, and dementia diagnosis was assigned by dementia-expert clinicians, after reviewing the cognitive tests' score and select clinical data, based on published criteria 36.
table.formatted: Participants completed 21 cognitive tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> , and dementia diagnosis was assigned by dementia-expert clinicians, after reviewing the cognitive tests' score and select clinical data, based on published criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36</ref>.

table.text: For example, an average participant had 40% of the examined area composed with type I muscle fibers, 22% with type II muscle fibers, 1% with mixed type I-II muscle fibers, and 37% with non-muscle fiber tissues.

Because the age range was relatively narrow, participants were mostly in their 9 th and 10th decades of life, we might have limited power to detect some of the aging effects previously reported, such as type I muscle fiber grouping, which were derived by comparing adults 20-40 years old with those older than 60 years 41 .
table.formatted: Because the age range was relatively narrow, participants were mostly in their 9 th and 10th decades of life, we might have limited power to detect some of the aging effects previously reported, such as type I muscle fiber grouping, which were derived by comparing adults 20-40 years old with those older than 60 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> .

table.text: For example, all participants had type I muscle fibers, but in 121 (51.3%) participants type IIX muscle fibers were not observed.

> For example, an average participant had 40% of the examined area composed with type I muscle fibers, 22% with type II muscle fibers, 1% with mixed type I-II muscle fibers, and 37% with non-muscle fiber tissues.

> For example, all participants had type I muscle fibers, but in 121 (51.3%) participants type IIX muscle fibers were not observed.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p=0.67", "p=0.051", "p=0.062", "p=0.097" ), Sentence = c("860.8 (SD=600.1), p<0.001)], whereas the relative counts of type II fibers did not differ by sex groups (p=0.67).", "In a compositional analysis including age at death and sex, males showed a higher relative proportion of type II fiber area in the quadriceps muscle while older age at death showed a borderline association (p=0.051) with a lower relative proportion of type II fiber area (Table", "In separate linear regressions that controlled for age at death, sex, and the time interval between the last measurement of physical activity and death, higher physical activity showed a borderline association (p=0.062) with a greater relative area composed of type II muscle fibers (Table 2).", "Higher physical activity had a borderline association (p=0.097) with more type II muscle fiber grouping." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

live_data_statements: The participants were from the Rush Memory and Aging Project (MAP), an ongoing longitudinal clinical pathologic cohort study recruiting community-dwelling older adults across northeastern Illinois since September 1997.
At annual visits, the participants were asked to walk 8 feet and turn 360 o twice.
Participants were also asked lower back pain and pain in the hip, knee, or feet that had lasted at least one month and had been present in most days.

Participants completed 21 cognitive tests 28, and dementia diagnosis was assigned by dementia-expert clinicians, after reviewing the cognitive tests' score and select clinical data, based on published criteria 36.

For example, an average participant had 40% of the examined area composed with type I muscle fibers, 22% with type II muscle fibers, 1% with mixed type I-II muscle fibers, and 37% with non-muscle fiber tissues.

Because the age range was relatively narrow, participants were mostly in their 9 th and 10th decades of life, we might have limited power to detect some of the aging effects previously reported, such as type I muscle fiber grouping, which were derived by comparing adults 20-40 years old with those older than 60 years 41 .
For example, all participants had type I muscle fibers, but in 121 (51.3%) participants type IIX muscle fibers were not observed.
